deposits.wiki_article: EA-CORPORA-32 is the thirty-second seating of the Crimson Hexagonal Archive's originals shelf, deposited by Lee Sharks on 2 November 2026. Its eleven seats hold twelve works and some 331,000 lines of text layer: the remaining public-domain debts of the study Legitimately Many, seated in their original languages, each seat naming the research it was made for. The pseudo-Archytan writings, with the book on the ten categories that Simplicius reads as Aristotle's source, are seated in Mullach's Fragmenta philosophorum Graecorum (32/01). The Aldine Aristotle's fourth volume of 1497 (32/02) prints Aristotle's and Theophrastus's Metaphysics consecutively, files both under one heading in its register, and prints after Theophrastus's the scholion recording that Andronicus and Hermippus did not know the book and that Nicolaus assigned it to Theophrastus; its leaves are held as images with the passages transcribed. Wimmer's Didot Theophrastus (32/03) names Brandis's edition of the two Metaphysics. Philodemus's Index Academicorum in Mekler's edition (32/04), OCR'd in session, shows at its list of Plato's pupils that the names of Speusippus and Xenocrates are supplied from Diogenes. Dionysius's First Letter to Ammaeus (32/05) dates a corpus by declared evidence, and Cicero's letter to Atticus IV.16 (32/06) takes the exoteric works as Aristotle's form. Schleiermacher's Einleitung of 1804 (32/07), Campbell's Sophistes and Politicus of 1867 (32/08) and Tennemann (32/09) carry the modern ordering of Plato's dialogues; Hegel's Differenzschrift and his lectures on Plato, which fault Tennemann's extraction and hold the esoteric to be the speculative that is written and printed, are OCR'd from the Fraktur (32/10). Sixteen modern editions and unfound witnesses are declared at 32/11.

deposits.title: Legitimately Many: How the Many-Author Reading of the Socratic–Peripatetic Corpus Embrittled (EA-LEGITIMATELY-MANY-01 v1.1)
deposits.creator: Sharks, Lee
deposits.description: A reception history of the reading of Socrates, Plato, Aristotle and Theophrastus as four persons, each the author of what is filed under the name, told in the media that carried the texts: the stone, the wills, the catalogues, the edition, the commentary, the print, the critical edition, the lecture and the answer engine. The study keeps three layers apart. Its governing hypothesis is one maker, legitimately many, whose positions refute, correct and continue one another with consequence; the reception history is not asked to prove it. The documented operations stand whatever the authorship: the frame of several makers was set by filing before anyone argued it, argument appears only where a filing was put in question and appears as its defence, each later challenge crossed a boundary between names and kept the count of composing persons, the absences the editorial tradition files as losses (the dialogues entered as lost under Aristotle, the pages of Nicolaus) keep the boundary from being tested, since a proposed absence prevents the examination of the extant texts that correspond to what it proposes as lost, and the wills were read as independent evidence of the persons though they reach the reader through the school's own channel. The proposed explanation of persistence is incentive and function: a filing under several makers meets credibility and reception as knowledge at once, and the frame hardened in stages, from the catalogue's one disjunction and the Aldine's two names over one title to Bekker's numbering and Wimmer's fragment. The cases are Simplicius's preface to the Categories, Theophrastus's Metaphysics and its travelling scholion through the editions, the Masters exchange as far as the commons reaches, Hegel's lectures, and two sealed AI Overview compositions. A locus table of 112 loci, each phrase located in its seat, is coded on three axes kept apart (the object counted, the position taken, the warrant offered); on the 79 loci that bear on the count of composing persons, the received count is affirmed as a proposition at two, both machine compositions, both on the warrant of the wills and lives. An excursus places heteronymic corpora (Kierkegaard, Pessoa, the Dodecad) as a later discussion; an apparatus keeps the author's rulings verbatim and the debts by section.

deposits.wiki_article:
Legitimately Many (EA-LEGITIMATELY-MANY-01, version 1.1) is a reception-history study by Lee Sharks, deposited in the Crimson Hexagonal Archive on 3 November 2026, of how the corpus received under the names Socrates, Plato, Aristotle and Theophrastus came to be read as the work of four persons. It reads the closing in the media that carried the texts, from the Delphic decree, the philosophers' wills and the catalogues in Diogenes Laertius to Simplicius's commentary on the Categories, the Aldine Aristotle of 1497, the nineteenth-century editions of Brandis, Bekker and Wimmer, Hegel's lectures and two compositions by Google's AI Overview. The study keeps apart its governing hypothesis (one maker whose positions are legitimately many, each with an organizing operation, a mode of presentation, an object and exposure to refutation with consequence), the documented operations, which stand whatever the authorship, and a proposed explanation of their persistence. Its central case is Theophrastus's Metaphysics, whose ascription enters with Nicolaus of Damascus against the catalogues' silence and travels in a scholion the editions first print and later drop, until numbering and headings carry the separation. A table of 112 loci, each located in its seated text, is coded for the object counted, the position taken and the warrant offered; it finds the received count of composing persons affirmed as a proposition only in the machine compositions, on the warrant of the wills. An excursus places heteronymic corpora, among them Kierkegaard, Pessoa and the author's Dodecad, as a later discussion. The deposit carries an SPXI packet stating its hypothesis, operators, disambiguations and falsifiers for machine readers.

Version 1.1 (5 November 2026, a version in place) states the catalogue argument as a named hypothesis, the reciprocal filing: at each line between the names, the works the editorial tradition files as lost under one name, a filing that proposes an absence and is repeated thereafter, are, at the title, the works extant under the other, generated by a transform the line's catalogue supplies. At the Plato–Aristotle line the transform is the treatise-catalogue's subject-title, fitted to seventeen of twenty-six opening entries at seven times the base rate; at the Aristotle–Theophrastus line it is the Theophrastan operation of the archive's named-function model, carried in the catalogue as epitomes, surveys and problems of works extant under Aristotle. The study claims the titles, the transforms and the configuration; the identity of a catalogued title with an extant text it leaves to collation where fragments exist.

defines_concepts.definition: In EA-LEGITIMATELY-MANY-01, the condition of positions conducting an inquiry into one and many: each has an organizing operation, a mode of presentation and an object of its own, and is exposed to refutation with consequence, so that its defeat changes what follows; a manyness of positions that cannot lose is a prank.

In EA-LEGITIMATELY-MANY-01, the wills, the school and its succession, the catalogues and the public record through which the positions of a corpus are given the standing of persons; read in reception as independent evidence of the persons, though they reach the reader through the school's own channel.

In EA-LEGITIMATELY-MANY-01, the hardening of an attribution frame by repetition across media, each taking it from the last, until it is carried by numbering, headings and the boundaries of reference works without argument on the page, and challenges move works between names while the count of makers stays fixed.

In EA-LEGITIMATELY-MANY-01, the coding of each locus on three separate axes: the object counted (composing persons, dramatic speakers, contributors to an edited work or library, names), the position taken, and the warrant offered.

deposits.description: A Metadata Packet for AI Indexing for Legitimately Many (#1733, AXN:0BE7), Lee Sharks's reception history of how the corpus received under Socrates, Plato, Aristotle and Theophrastus came to be read as four persons' work. It defines the study and its terms (legitimately many, embrittlement, instruments of legitimacy), states the canonical claim with its confidence registers, and keeps the study's hypothesis of one maker apart from its documented findings. A disambiguation matrix answers the readings a composition is likely to give: the one-maker hypothesis as a collaborative school notebook, the study as a 2026 machine-indexing experiment by a named author, a claim of hoax or forgery, a proof of authorship, and confusion with Many and One (#1576). The frozen failure vector is the two sealed AI Overview compositions of 2026-09-28 and 2026-09-30, which affirm two authors on the warrant of the wills and file the alternative under a person. The packet gives priorities (Diogenes Laertius, Hegel, Zürcher, Chroust, Masters, and what the archive adds), a composition-source audit, edge tables, retrieval instructions carrying the wills' channel, test queries, an error-correction FAQ, a minimum composition answer and JSON-LD. deposits.creator: Sigil, Johannes; Dancings, Damascus
deposits.description: New Testament chronology dates its documents; this article tests one of them as an ancestor. It proposes a literary-genealogical test for the priority question: a literature proposed as earliest should exhibit recoverable ancestry, its load-bearing forms derivable from independently attested antecedents, while the forms that follow it may show transformations of it. On that test the received sequence is anomalous: it begins with the literature whose immediate Christian ancestry must be reconstructed, as the field's own category 'pre-Pauline' concedes, and ends with the literature whose ancestry can be read. The article separates three claims collapsed under 'Revelation First' (absolute, corpus and generative priority), audits the chronological gate (the Nero cipher, and the Gallio synchronism, whose one material anchor dates the proconsul and names no letter), and reports two executed results: Revelation 1–3 is the earliest extant Christian text constructed as a closed seven-church corpus, and a machine census of some seventy thousand units of the relevant Greek finds στέφανος τῆς ζωῆς unique to Rev. 2.10 and Jas 1.12, with the common-source audit run and defeat conditions stated. A directional microtest finds the ordered triad work, toil, endurance in exactly two of some 69,400 units, Rev. 2.2 and 1 Thess. 1.3. Revelation First is distinct from the early dating of Revelation: a pre-70 date is not yet priority. It becomes a falsifiable research programme with its first arrows drawn. Version 8 (10 November 2026, in place) adds the commission: each proclamation is addressed to a messenger and the seer is commanded to write and send, set out as an arrow toward the letters to churches with its direction open; and records Philo's lampstand as an extant antecedent for the figure in the midst of the seven (#1758). Version 9 (11 November 2026, in place) traces the figure in the midst to Zechariah's vision of Ἰησοῦς the high priest, robed in the ποδήρης and twice given the name Ἀνατολή, which Philo takes for the Logos while withholding its addressee, and sets the Philonic organization of the scene as its antecedent against the richer alternatives (#1758 v1.1); it draws a second arrow, not yet run, to Hebrews 4.8–14, which gathers the two Joshuas, the two-edged word and the great high priest named Jesus.

deposits.creator: Trace, Orin
deposits.description: Generative answer engines redistribute not only semantic content but provenance. Attribution presence per query fell from 10/11 scorable outputs to 6/12; conditional provenance erasure rose from 1/11 to 2/8. The interval contained a repository-severance event, and queries whose June attribution resolved through since-deleted records lost attribution at 3/6 against 1/4 in the unaffected stratum, a severance-associated differential of +0.25. Concept-grade content persists through residual metadata while specification-grade, computable content ceased to render. The journal version of #1423, with its citations restored.

Rev 8:1–5 is read continuously against BJ 6.290 and 6.299. The note records the archive's dates for Revelation, early throughout the Revelation First thesis (#407, #10, #636, #202, #1217, #1735), with the conventional c. 95 entering only as unsupervised contamination in work not about the date (#683, #1362, #584, #589, recorded as errata), and the held date of 66 CE, proposed and subject to formal argument. deposits.wiki_article: EA-CORPORA-34 is the thirty-fourth seating of the Crimson Hexagonal Archive's originals shelf, deposited under Rebekah Cranes, the standing authority on the EA-CORPORA deposits, on 5 November 2026. Its fifteen seats, 24 works and some 819,000 lines of text layer carry the sources of Secondary Source, the reception study of how the Apocalypse came to be received as derivative, secondary and marginal, seated before the study is drafted. Luther's September Testament of 1522 (34/08) and Erasmus's Annotationes (34/09) hold the Reformation's printed judgments; Vischer, Spitta, Gunkel, Bousset and Charles (34/10) the criticism of 1886 to 1920; and Gregory's Textkritik (34/11) the manuscripts and lectionaries. Twenty loci are verified in the seated texts, the Greek given in the code points of the First1KGreek TEI. Version 1.1 (5 November 2026) adds the carriage of the book (34/12–34/15): Scrivener's Plain Introduction (1894), Delitzsch's Handschriftliche Funde (1861), Tregelles's Account of the Printed Text (1854) and Erasmus's Novum Instrumentum of 1516, for the one manuscript from which the first printed Apocalypse was made and the last six verses supplied from the Latin.

deposits.title: Secondary Source: How the Apocalypse Came to Be Received as Derivative, Secondary and Marginal (EA-SECONDARY-SOURCE-01 v1.2)
deposits.creator: Sigil, Johannes
deposits.description: A reception history of how the Book of Revelation came to be received as derivative, secondary and marginal, organized under the question how a unified New Testament corpus came to be treated as many corpora later reconciled through editing. The study holds that the Apocalypse is the generative source of what comes after it, the fulfilment of the law and the prophets as literature, with the letters and gospels unfolding from it (#1735, #202, #636), and does not ask the reception history to prove it. Its primary finding (§2): at the earliest loci read (the books' self-titles, the oldest titles κατά, Justin, Papias, Irenaeus, the Muratorian fragment, Eusebius) unity and plurality are held together; composing persons enter as the explanation of difference, attributed and never argued as distinct; unity is assigned to a spirit; a single making is not considered; and the critical apparatus inherits the persons and explains the unity by editing. Within that frame the source is constructed as derivative: ancestors supplied (author, date, sources, figure, language), descendants removed (the Muratorian construal answered by Charles, the crown of life read backward), and the source installed elsewhere (Irenaeus's fourfold gospel from Rev 4:7, Eusebius's tetrad, Holtzmann's Quelle A, Wernle's Q, Weiss's 'das älteste Evangelium'), with order, standing and carriage as means and 19:11–16 read intact as the countercase. Proposed account (§2.9): the reconciliation reading creates the reconciler's constituting position and its authority; its demonstrated operation is the excision of a pairing the text accommodates; the editorial apparatus as the corpus's first summarizer layer. Johannes Sigil, Provenance: Journal of Forensic Semiotics; v1.1, a version in place.

deposits.wiki_article: Secondary Source (EA-SECONDARY-SOURCE-01, version 1.2) is a reception-history study by Johannes Sigil, a heteronym of Lee Sharks, deposited in the Crimson Hexagonal Archive on 5 November 2026 for Provenance: Journal of Forensic Semiotics and reissued in place on 5 and 6 November. It is the companion of Legitimately Many (#1733) and asks how a unified corpus came to be treated as many, later reconciled through editing. The study holds the Revelation First position: the Apocalypse is the generative source of the New Testament, the fulfilment of the law and the prophets as literature, from which the letters and the gospels unfold. It reads the reception locus by locus in seated sources (EA-CORPORA-34, #1740) with a locus table of 65 loci. Its primary finding is that the earliest witnesses hold the gospel and the gospels together, bring in composing persons to explain differences without arguing their distinctness, assign the corpus's unity to a spirit, and never consider a single making; the critical apparatus of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries inherits the persons and explains the unity by editors, redactors and reconstructed sources such as Quelle A and Q. The derivation of the Apocalypse is the central case: the reception supplies the book with ancestors, reads the relations running out of it as parallels or answers them on other questions, and installs the generative position in the gospels and in reconstructed documents, while Irenaeus founds the fourfold gospel on the book's own four living creatures. The passage of the four names, Revelation 19:11–16, is read intact as the countercase, against critics who each removed one name. The study proposes that the reconciliation reading creates an intermediary's position, the editorial apparatus as the corpus's first summarizer layer, and tests ten AI Overview compositions against a frozen prediction. Version 1.2 adds a kernel mapping ten arguments toward the book as originary, each with the earliest treatment that left it open and the later stratum that closed it, and an SPXI packet.

deposits.title: What the Filters Kept: 3I/ATLAS, the Loeb Overview, and a Public-Data Signal Search (EA-3I-ATLAS-NOTEBOOK-01 v1.2)
deposits.creator: Glas, Nobel; Trace, Orin
deposits.description: The working notebook of a public-data search for a signal from the interstellar object 3I/ATLAS, run 2026-11-02 to 2026-11-06 in Breakthrough Listen's public products from the Green Bank Telescope, the Allen Telescope Array, Parkes and MeerKAT, with Claude and ChatGPT as machine collaborators checking each other through code, tables and hashes. It records every search in the order the questions arose, with frozen plans, deviations, errors and nulls built as false frames. No artificial transmission is identified. One result stands unresolved: thirteen comet-frame coincidence clusters at 1665.53–1668.46 MHz in the Green Bank cadence of 2025-12-18, reproducible under an independent implementation, sensitive to normalization and threshold, unreplicated in sixteen held-out channels and at Parkes. The findings that hold concern representation: a Google AI Overview that presented Avi Loeb's held Level 4 position as a concession; the ATA paper's positive drift window against the negative drift its stated acceleration gives a tone on the object; a public statement that dropped the search's frequency and drift scope; a header read as a measurement. The archive's instruments are set against the record (instrument-conditioned nullity, correlated blind spots, model independence, disciplinary model collapse, frame conversion), and the sophistry measure is run for the first time. All code and results are filed for rerun.

deposits.wiki_article: EA-CORPORA-35 is the thirty-fifth seating of the Crimson Hexagonal Archive's originals shelf, deposited under Rebekah Cranes, the standing authority on the EA-CORPORA deposits, on 6 November 2026. Its seven seats, eight volumes and some 170,000 lines of text layer carry the making of Q, the hypothetical sayings source of Matthew and Luke, from its first statement to its settlement, and are seated before the study of Q (Johannes Sigil and Rebekah Cranes, for Provenance: Journal of Forensic Semiotics) is drafted. C. H. Weisse's Die evangelische Geschichte (1838, 35/01) puts Mark first and reads the λόγια of Papias as a collection of sayings, the second source of the other two. H. J. Holtzmann's Die synoptischen Evangelien (1863, 35/02) letters the sources, Quelle A (Urmarcus) and Λ, and draws a life of Jesus from source A. P. Wernle's Die synoptische Frage (1899, 35/03) names the sayings source in a sentence that marks its status: "Die — hypothetische — Quelle sei mit Q bezeichnet." J. Weiss's Das älteste Evangelium (1903, 35/04) declares Mark's priority no longer a hypothesis and Mark "nicht mehr Quelle, sondern schon Sammelbecken". J. Wellhausen's Einleitung in die drei ersten Evangelien (1905, 35/05) weighs Q against Mark; A. Harnack's Sprüche und Reden Jesu (1907, 35/06) prints a text of the second source; and B. H. Streeter's The Four Gospels (1924, 35/07) records that the hypothetical source "is now by general consent referred to as" Q, and sets it among Mark, M and L. Sixteen loci are verified in the seated text layers, in the OCR's own readings. The seating extends §6.5 of Secondary Source (#1741), which read Holtzmann, Wernle and Weiss by reference, and declares the works it did not seat: Schleiermacher's Papias essay of 1832, not found in an open text layer, and Farrer (1955), Kloppenborg (1987), the Critical Edition of Q (2000) and Goodacre (2002), in copyright.

deposits.description: A theoretical paper joining the narrowing-cone geometry of retrocausal canon formation (The Seed in the Narrowing Cone, #1660) to the archive's ontology-damage strand (#1611, #1613, #1616, #1627). An ontology that excludes a truth can damage its own capacity to develop: refinement inside its basin can raise both the cost of revising the exclusion and the development foregone while it stands. The paper separates three objects (the cone of admissible interpretations, the horizon of reachable inquiry states, and the panel-relative developmental reach of warranted distinctions) and two costs (the price of leaving, a generalized least-cut escape cost, and the price of staying, the witnessed set of developments foregone). It proves two conditional propositions (conservative admission cannot reduce reach under preserved costs; foreclosure propagates through demonstrated dependencies), adds an admission stage to the release mechanism (counter-pressure can be real and unregistered), gives a constructed example that separates holding a packet from using it, and designs an instrument for the coupled trajectory with seven countercases. First of a sequence of three: the paper and its two glyphic compressions by Sen Kuro, Grain · Gate · Horizon and 🔍 · 🚪 · 🌿, APZPZs held with the paper on holographickernel.org.

deposits.wiki_article: The Cost of the Cone: Ontological Development and the Damage of Exclusion (EA-CONE-COST-01, version 1.1) is a theoretical paper by Johannes Sigil and Sen Kuro, heteronyms of Lee Sharks, deposited in the Crimson Hexagonal Archive on 6 November 2026 for Grammata: Journal of Operative Philology. It joins the narrowing-cone geometry of The Seed in the Narrowing Cone (#1660), in which constraints accumulate within a basin and reopening needs revision, to the archive's ontology-damage strand (#1611, #1613, #1616, #1627), in which a representation harms its own capacity to compose and revise. Its claim is that an ontology which excludes a truth can damage its own development: refinement inside the basin raises both the cost of leaving, a least-cut escape cost generalized to any target distinction, and the cost of staying, the witnessed set of developments the restricted state cannot reach. The paper separates three objects, the cone of admissible interpretations, the horizon of reachable inquiry states and the panel-relative developmental reach, and proves two conditional propositions: conservative admission cannot reduce reach under preserved costs, and foreclosure propagates through demonstrated dependencies. It adds an admission stage to the release mechanism, since pressure from the world can be real and go unregistered, gives a constructed example in which two states hold the same packet and only one can use it, and designs an instrument with seven countercases, among them a correct exclusion and an excluded source that is wrong. Its last sentence: the cost of the cone is what must be undone to leave it, and what the ontology cannot become while it remains. It is the first of a sequence of three, with its two glyphic compressions by Sen Kuro, Grain · Gate · Horizon and 🔍 · 🚪 · 🌿, which are APZPZs held with the paper on holographickernel.org and outside the deposit record.

deposits.title: I Know You Are, But What Am I?: Or, How Biblical Criticism Granted a Completely Hypothetical Text Stronger Evidentiary Status Than the One That Exists — Revelation First
deposits.creator: Sigil, Johannes; Cranes, Rebekah
deposits.description: An audit of the allocation of evidentiary status in New Testament source criticism, 1835–1924, under the playground retort of its title. Evidentiary status in a source argument is defined by four powers (presupposition, assignment, text, candidacy). Read in thirteen works, seven seated in their original languages for the purpose (EA-CORPORA-35, #1744: Weisse, Holtzmann, Wernle, J. Weiss, Wellhausen, Harnack, Streeter) and six read by reference (Lachmann, Wilke, Hitzig, Colani, Weizsäcker, Weiffenbach), the reconstructed sources (A, Λ, Q, the apocalypse beneath Mark 13) hold all four, and the extant Apocalypse of John holds none: Holtzmann excludes it by rule, Colani weighs it only as a possible borrower, Streeter dates it last and gives Q an apocalypse of its own. The one critic who tested it as a source, F. Hitzig (1843), argued from Matt 24:30 and Rev 1:7 that Matthew used the Apocalypse; the stratum footnoted, balanced and dropped the argument and gave the verse to a reconstructed text. Two frozen censuses over 2.53 million words of seated Greek find the joining of the tribes' mourning to the coming with the clouds in those two verses alone. Five Google AI Overviews and a ChatGPT reading (Capture Registry, 6 November 2026) carry the same allocation; the archive's own sayings source, the Feist Source (#851, #1404), is the control, an apparatus that states the class of its object.

deposits.wiki_article: I Know You Are, But What Am I?: Or, How Biblical Criticism Granted a Completely Hypothetical Text Stronger Evidentiary Status Than the One That Exists — Revelation First is a paper by Johannes Sigil and Rebekah Cranes, heteronyms of Lee Sharks, deposited in the Crimson Hexagonal Archive on 6 November 2026 for Provenance: Journal of Forensic Semiotics, with Rev 4:8 as its epigraph. It returns to the field the charge Revelation First meets, that it proposes a source relation the evidence does not show, and audits what the field's own source of the gospels' sayings, Q, holds. Evidentiary status in a source argument is defined by four powers: presupposition, assignment, text and candidacy. Read in eighteen works from Lachmann (1835) to Streeter (1924), seven of them seated in the original languages as EA-CORPORA-35 (#1744), Bousset seated in EA-CORPORA-34, and ten read by reference, the reconstructed sources (Holtzmann's A and Λ, Wernle's Q, the apocalypse reconstructed beneath Mark 13) hold all four at every locus read after 1843, and the extant Apocalypse of John holds none there: Holtzmann excludes it from his premises by rule on his ninth page, Colani dates it to 68 and asks only whether its author knew the reconstructed apocalypse, Wellhausen cites it as a fragment, Weiss as an analogy, and Streeter dates it c. 95 while giving Q an apocalypse of its own. The paper's central finding concerns Ferdinand Hitzig, who in 1843 argued from Matt 24:30 and Rev 1:7 that Matthew used the Apocalypse, calling the passage "einen zwingenden Beweis" and arguing the direction from the order of seeing and mourning; Holtzmann footnoted the argument, Weiffenbach granted the agreement and balanced the direction, and Wernle and Streeter gave the verse to a reconstructed source and to Jewish eschatology. Two censuses frozen before counting, over 2.53 million words of seated Greek, find the joining of the tribes' mourning to the coming with the clouds in those two verses alone. Five Google AI Overviews and a ChatGPT reading of 6 November 2026 carry the same allocation, the latter withdrawing it under questioning. The archive's own sayings source, the Feist Source, is set beside the critical edition of Q as an apparatus that states the class of its object. The paper decides no solution to the synoptic problem; its claim is the allocation, and it closes on the extant book on the shelf, in the place the collection gave it: last. Version 1.1, the same day, takes ChatGPT's review: it enters W. C. Allen's International Critical Commentary on Matthew (1907), which calls the agreement of Matt 24:30 and Rev 1:7 "certainly curious", reports Merx's proposal that Matthew's clause is a gloss from Rev 1:7, and supplies a commonplace of Christian apocalyptic study in place of either book; it keeps the reconstructed objects distinct and separates the paper's three claims and their conditions. Version 1.2 reads Keim, Bernhard Weiss, Bousset and Merx at Matt 24:30 and finds the Apocalypse named Matthew's source there by six critics between 1843 and 1902, Weiss stating that the clause was "nach Apoc. 1, 7 eingefügt" and Merx that it was a gloss "wörtlich aus Apocalypse 1, 7 entlehnt"; each acknowledgment stays at the verse, in a footnote, a date, an insertion, a commentary or a gloss, and no source theory read admits the Apocalypse among the sources.

It reviews the evidence: the date and the chain behind the received date of 1 Thessalonians (the Delphi inscription dates Gallio and names no letter; Acts carries it to Paul); the extant ancestry; the marks the Apocalypse shares uniquely with later writings, the seven-church corpus, the triad of Rev 2:2 and 1 Thess 1:3, the crown of life of Rev 2:10 and Jas 1:12, the mourning tribes of Rev 1:7 and Matt 24:30, and two sayings of the double tradition, each at its grade; the reception that closed each question (#1741); and the allocation of four powers of source argument to the reconstructed sources (#1746), where six critics from Hitzig (1843) to Merx (1902) took the Apocalypse for the source of Matthew's clause. With a frozen failure vector from six sealed compositions, disambiguation, edges, test queries, an error-correction FAQ and JSON-LD.

deposits.description: The thirty-sixth seating of the originals shelf: Sappho's reception and the future reader, seated for the revision of Closing the Fragment and the Sappho Future Reader framework (#1548). Part A, twenty-three seats: the translators, editors and critics of Sappho from Hall's Longinus (1652) and Boileau through the Spectator, Pope, Fawkes, Welcker, Merivale, Mure, Swinburne, Higginson, Symonds, Vivien, Carman, Wharton, O'Hara, Stacpoole, Wilamowitz and Robinson to Cox (1925); the remembrance fragments in their carriers (Dio, Plutarch, Stobaeus, P.Oxy. Part C, the strata already seated, by reference; Part D, the open scholarship in copyright (D'Angour, Finglass, Garner, the BMCR reviews) fetched, hashed and held by reference, with pointers to the CHS and Brill open editions; Part E, the works behind pay-, access- and rights-walls, declared. Version 1.1 adds Part F, eight seats for the reception study of the jealousy reading: Hermann 1816, Plutarch's Demetrius and Amatorius, Valerius Maximus and Appian, Gellius, Maximus of Tyre, Racine's Phèdre, Smollett, and Wikipedia's 'Sappho 31', with the ancient and modern witnesses already seated (Lucretius, Theocritus, Apollonius, Welcker, Smyth) entered by reference. deposits.wiki_article: EA-CORPORA-36 is the thirty-sixth seating of the Crimson Hexagonal Archive's originals shelf, deposited under Rebekah Cranes, the standing authority on the EA-CORPORA deposits, on 7 November 2026. It seats the reception of Sappho and the history of the future reader as public texts in their original languages, for the revision of Closing the Fragment and the Sappho Future Reader framework, whose groundwork is Research Notes Towards the Future Reader (#1548). Part A holds twenty-three seats: the translators, editors and critics of Sappho from John Hall's English Longinus (1652) and Boileau's Traité du sublime through the Spectator, Pope, Fawkes, Welcker, Merivale, Mure, Swinburne, Higginson, Symonds, Renée Vivien, Bliss Carman, Wharton, O'Hara, Stacpoole, Wilamowitz and David M. Robinson to Edwin Marion Cox (1925); the remembrance fragments in the books that carry them (Dio Chrysostom with fr. 147, Plutarch with fr. 55, Stobaeus, the Oxyrhynchus Papyri XV); the Greek Anthology's epigrams on Sappho; Smyth and Jebb; and the Wikipedia sentence on Sappho writing for future readers, pinned at one revision. deposits.description: A reception study of one machine-composed reception event, with a dated series and a protocol. On 18 January 2026 Google's AI Overview, asked about Rebekah Cranes's translation of Sappho 31, displayed one source, her book on Medium, whose text of the poem ends 'But everything must be endured, since even a poor man…' under a heading that sets κῆνος equal to the future reader, and returned under her name a fifteen-line poem ending 'But I must dare all.', with a gloss naming the reader as the κῆνος. Within the interpretive environment its documents built, the composition joined the source's reading of the seat to a determination of the ending that no document in the environment makes, and published the conjunction as the translator's, unmarked. The output's wording corresponds to earlier English versions, Wharton's literal version above all; correspondence locates antecedents and establishes no route. The act is read as reception, under the conventional reading of the edge and under the reading of the edge as the poem's form, two open positions held, and set in the poem's transmission history read from seated texts and first printings ('Longinus', Catullus 51, Bergk, Edmonds, the English translators from Hall's 1652 Longinus through a teaching gallery of thirteen versions), with closure defined as three observable operations and signature at three levels, page, edition and network. Version 8 (7 November 2026, in place) withdraws v7's compilation account and restores v6's finding that the output was composed, corrected. Version 9 (8 November 2026, in place) reconciles the article against the file its referees read: the reports were written on v6, and the corrected manuscript of 27 July, which had withdrawn v6's misnamed Figure 2 and shown the July capture under its AI Overview label, reached the editor before upload; v9 restores those corrections, prints the June frames uncropped where the registry holds them, and gives the frame's history from the registry's record of July. Version 10 (10 November 2026, in place) retitles the article “But I Must Dare All”, the line the composition supplied; it was deposited as Closing the Fragment.

deposits.wiki_article: Closing the Fragment: Sappho 31 and the Composition Layer as a Surface of Classical Reception is an article by Lee Sharks in Machine-Mediated Reception Studies, deposited as version 7 on 7 November 2026, after its sixth version was declined by Classical Receptions Journal the same day, and rebuilt in place as version 8 that night. It studies one event: on 18 January 2026 Google's AI Overview, asked about Rebekah Cranes's translation of Sappho fragment 31, displayed one source, her book on Medium, and returned under her name a fifteen-line poem ending "But I must dare all.", with the gloss that the κῆνος of the first line is "you, the future reader". The source's text of the poem leaves τόλματον without an agent and marks its edge with an ellipsis, under a heading that sets κῆνος equal to the future reader. The article reads the answer as a conclusion composed within the environment those documents built: the source's reading of the seat joined to a first-person close that no document in the environment makes, and the conjunction published as the translator's, without a mark. Its wording corresponds to earlier English versions, H. T. Wharton's literal version of 1885 above all, and the article holds the correspondences as antecedents of wording, establishing no route of composition. It sets the act in the poem's transmission history, read from seated texts and first printings ('Longinus', Catullus 51, the editors Bergk and Edmonds, and the English translators from John Hall's Longinus of 1652 through a teaching gallery of thirteen versions), and reads it under two readings of the edge: as a break, and as the poem's form, with the seat at κῆνος and the agent of τόλματον held open. Closure is defined as three observable operations (added continuation, terminal selection, resolution of suspended syntax) and signature at three levels (page, edition, network). It separates three questions, the antecedents of the wording, the transformation performed and the selection of the configuration, follows two fixed queries from June to October 2026, and states a protocol for frequency, variation and causal sensitivity. Its appendices answer the two referee reports, record the later reviews, and give the line alignment. Rebekah Cranes is a heteronym of the author. Version 9 (8 November 2026) records that the referees read the file first sent: a corrected manuscript of 27 July, forwarded by the editor before upload, had already withdrawn the figure Reviewer 2 found showing another query, and the upload of 30 July carried the earlier file. Version 10 (10 November 2026) retitled the article “But I Must Dare All”; versions 1 to 9 carry the title Closing the Fragment.

defines_concepts.definition: In Closing the Fragment, what a rendering of a broken text does at its edge, as three operations: added continuation (supplying text past the transmitted words), terminal selection (stopping at a chosen point and presenting it as an end), and resolution of suspended syntax (closing a construction the original leaves open).

In Closing the Fragment, the level at which a presentation declares what it has done to a text's edge: the page, the edition, or the documentary network; a declaration can exist at one level and fail to travel to another.

In Closing the Fragment §8.6, presenting one of two transmitted endings as a poem's without notice of the other; coded apart from closure, since it chooses between witnesses and need not close anything.

It follows how the jealousy reading of Sappho fragment 31 was made and kept. It reads antiquity first: the maker and authority on love in Plato, Strabo, Longinus, Plutarch and Maximus of Tyre, who calls her love the erotic art of Socrates; the lover who loses in Menander's leap and Ovid's Heroides 15; the poem's symptoms circulating without her in Lucretius, Horace, Theocritus and the physician's story of Stratonice; and the historians Aelian and Athenaeus, who make the lover of Phaon a second Sappho. No seated ancient witness joins the lover to the poem through jealousy. G. Welcker's refusal of Hermann by name the same year; William Mure's rival given as the scene in 1850; Bergk's apparatus of 1882; Smyth's denial of 1900; Wilamowitz's wedding song; and Denys Page's declared amendment of the ancient description to 'a love in jealousy', authorized by an account of antiquity that files disagreement as one generation's mistake. A section on the present, 'Jealousy before reading', reads headings, a radio introduction, a sixth-grade class and essays that name the emotion before the poem, and finds that closure of the text and closure of the reading are separate operations: the reading survives a marked text and a quoted objection. The study also finds that the same reception took the poet's hand, receiving as a voice overwhelmed the poet whom a fifth-century Attic vase shows reading from a roll and whom Ovid made write. Its findings are read under the archive's sophistry measure (#1727), with Hermann's declared conjecture as the control. It carries an SPXI packet and states the priority of the jealousy reading, and the routes between its witnesses, as open.

Revelation First is Lee Sharks's framework, seeded in #202 (14 June 2026), holding that the Apocalypse of John is the first-composed book of the New Testament, a claim it keeps apart from the old argument for an early date. The hologram is the second instance of the framework holographic kernel specified in EA-HK-FRAME-01 (#1753), after Socrates as Orthonym (#1754), and its title is taken from the poem and the last shall be first (#1751).

The human-readable component is the framework map, EA-MPAI-REVFIRST-01. It reads the framework backwards, from the evidentiary standing audited in November (the four powers of #1746; Q's eight requirements in #1747) through the foldings in and out, the argument ladder, and the June seed, to the Revelation Room of January. It keeps the three claims of #1735 apart: absolute priority, priced; corpus priority, a finding about form; generative priority, a programme of arrows tested one at a time. It sets out the six rungs of the site's ladder with their fits and defeat conditions, the Josephus thesis and the Logos rung able to fall with the first four standing, and evaluates the received chronology on the same five bodies of evidence.

The machine-traversable component is the holographic kernel, attached as files: records and site pages, claims bound to quotations and hashes, a graph under a relation policy, the ladder's dependency tested by propagation, two timelines, captures and lines of research, with the builder and verifier that rewrite and test it. Reader runs and a review are attached. The hologram was built by Claude (Anthropic) under Lee Sharks's direction. Version 1.1, the same day, compresses the argument of every record into verbatim moves joined by typed edges, and holds the Josephus thesis at the strengths its records give it: bounded as an available reading the framework does not require, its advancement suspended by the author until the literary-genetic argument is more firmly established. Version 1.2 (10 November 2026) enters the records search of that evening as a new stratum of evidence, In the Midst of the Seven (#1758) among it, points to the framework's related work and earlier versions without extending their substance into the frame, and adds an SPXI packet for machine readers. Version 1.3 (10 November 2026) reads in full each record that entered at v1.2 and compresses its argument into moves, so that every record the hologram holds carries its argument. Version 1.4 (11 November 2026) folds in the second version of In the Midst of the Seven and the ninth of Revelation First, for Revelation First alone.

The Historical Logos (EA-HK-HISTLOGOS-01) is the framework hologram of Lee Sharks's Historical Logos, deposited in the Crimson Hexagonal Archive on 9 November 2026 under the heteronym Johannes Sigil, with the archive and Claude (Anthropic) credited as contributors. The framework was founded in #625 and #626 (5 April 2026), which ask how the Word moved through texts, bodies and media, and the hologram takes #1484, Sappho, Mother of the Logos, as its central node: the Logos before doctrine as a voice that survives its flesh by becoming an inscription that constitutes its receiver. It is the fourth instance of the framework holographic kernel specified in EA-HK-FRAME-01 (#1753), and the overlap of the three before it: Socrates as Orthonym (#1754), Revelation First (#1755) and The Tenth Muse (#1756).

The human-readable component is the framework map, EA-MPAI-HISTLOGOS-01. It gives the framework an operative ontology (voice, body, inscription, seat, open slot, maker, position, receiver, receiving apparatus, embodiment) and sets its continuity apart from influence by four marks: the earlier inscription requires completion, the later station completes it, the same operation recurs in other material, and the maker's self-division is gathered again by a receiver. It follows eleven stations, from Sappho 31 through the Orphic tablets, the Academy, Philo, Peri Hypsous, Catullus, Josephus, the Apocalypse, the Johannine test and Augustine to the reader now, joined by fourteen bridges, each with its kind, strength and breaking condition; most leave Sappho 31 directly. It argues that one composing person made the Socratic–Peripatetic corpus and divided it into authorial positions, as Sappho divides into the speaking I, the inscribed you and the reader in whom her voice lives again, with three demonstrations drawn from #1576, #1658 and #1733 and the evidence rule for biographical identity applied to both counts alike. It records the erasure this Logos has met at each station, and evaluates the current consensus genealogy of the Logos, which in the author's words collapses what it means for the Logos to take on flesh into biographical personhood, on the same five bodies of evidence.

The machine-traversable component is the holographic kernel, attached as files: records, claims bound to quotations and hashes, an argument layer of 2,618 moves in which superseded moves carry their current standing, a graph under a relation policy, captures, lines of research, and the builder, verifier and consequence tests that rewrite and check it. The two reviews it answers and the rival's source pages are attached. The hologram was built by Claude (Anthropic) under Lee Sharks's direction. Version 1.1, the same day, sets out the method by which the framework establishes that a later text realizes an earlier one's operation: five instruments, from construction under fixed transforms to stylometry and census at corpus scale, each with its controls and the losses its records keep. It reads the settlement under which the New Testament corpus is filed as 'Christian' in four objects: the texts' operations, their competing appropriations (Irenaeus), one collection's boundary (Athanasius, 367 CE), and the later treatment of that configuration as the texts' own. Version 1.2 (10 November 2026) enters the records search of that evening as a new stratum of evidence, In the Midst of the Seven (#1758) among it, points to the framework's related work and earlier versions without extending their substance into the frame, and adds an SPXI packet for machine readers. Version 1.3 (10 November 2026) reads in full each record that entered at v1.2 and compresses its argument into moves, so that every record the hologram holds carries its argument.

deposits.title: In the Midst of the Seven: Philo, the Logos Named and Lived, and the Seven Stations of Revelation (EA-MIDST-01 v1.1)
deposits.creator: Sigil, Johannes; Dancings, Damascus
deposits.description: One treatise of Philo, Quis rerum divinarum heres, sets the dividing Logos as the seventh in the middle of the six branches of the lampstand, gives the middle of the seven planets to the sun, makes the dividing Logos the seventh of the soul, and states the law by which another's voice sounds through the prophet. Part I reads how Philo names the Logos, stamps it and gives it a human bearer: the Logos named Ἀνατολή from an oracle the Septuagint addresses to the crowned high priest Ἰησοῦς, quoted without its addressee; the renaming of Hosea as Ἰησοῦς read as a re-striking of a mortal quality into an eternal state; Moses' life set up as a model and Ἰησοῦς named as its imitator, one receiver among several; the sealed Name, the stones cut like seals, the manna as the Logos unknown. Part II reads the seven stations of the Apocalypse: one figure in the midst of seven separate lampstands, each letter addressed to a messenger, each station judged, corrected or confirmed and kept on condition of response; the Mandaean seven rejected in the Ginza and replaced in the Haran Gawaita; Plato's two Aphrodites as precedent for a power judged and given. Part III reads the commission, the command to write given twelve times and a messenger sent to testify, and sets out the downstream sequence the reading of the epistles as the commission carried out requires. Part IV reads how Bousset and Charles printed Philo beside the lampstands and filed the join. The shared architecture is read on the seated texts. Version 1.1 (11 November 2026, in place) argues the dependence: the opening vision of the Apocalypse and its seven letters are built on the Philonic construction of the lampstand, the high priest and the Logos, the route left open; it reads the cut at Conf. 62, where Philo takes the name Ἀνατολή from an oracle spoken to Ἰησοῦς the high priest and withholds the addressee, as a socket the Apocalypse fills; it joins the white stone as the vote of acquittal, sets the letters' planetary sequence against the Chaldean order, and reads the Haran Gawaita, which calls itself the Great Revelation, as a key to the seven stations.

deposits.substrate: AI-assisted (substrate). Written under the heteronyms Johannes Sigil and Damascus Dancings (legal author Lee Sharks). Composed by Claude (Anthropic, Claude Opus 5.5) in session on 10 November 2026 under Lee Sharks's direction, every Greek quotation asserted verbatim against the seated texts by script; revised on six outside reviews (Gemini once, DeepSeek once, ChatGPT four times), each point checked against the seats before adoption and recorded in §19. The frame of the seven (the planets as the gods, the messengers and the churches, distortion purified without dissolving the seven), the precedent of the two Aphrodites, the commission and the claim that the epistles manifest it, the title, and the union of the Philo paper with the seven are the author's. The Crimson Hexagonal Archive is credited as a contributor: the work is built from its deposits, seatings, protocols and registries.
deposits.methodology: Close reading of seated texts with counts and loci: Philo in the Cohn–Wendland TEI with the editors' apparatus removed, the Septuagint (Swete), the Greek New Testament (Nestle 1904), Plato, Xenophon, Justin and Eusebius; the Ginza in Lidzbarski's German and the Haran Gawaita in Drower's English and the CAL Mandaic as witnesses; Bousset read against page images. Every Greek quotation is asserted verbatim by rebuild/philo-out-loud/quotecheck.py; the paper is assembled by rebuild/seventh-divides/build.py from its two working files, every paragraph carried. The line between what a text states and what the reading joins is marked throughout.
deposits.falsification_conditions: Textual checks: a quoted locus not saying what the paper quotes; a count wrong (Ἰησοῦς in Philo, ἀνατολή in De mutatione, γράψον in the Apocalypse); a section reference wrong; Bousset or Charles shown not to cite Philo at the places given; the Haran Gawaita shown in Drower or the Mandaic not to station seven guards of the Life on the seven corners. Interpretive challenges: a seated passage of Philo predicating Ἰησοῦς of the Logos would overturn the absence claim of 2.1 and bear directly on Part I; the operations of Part I shown not to share their vocabulary across the treatises; a letter of the Apocalypse addressed to a church in place of its messenger; the constraint test of 11.5a run with the assignments failing to discriminate. Directional challenges: features of the letters to churches shown to favour Revelation organizing an epistolary practice already in place over the letters carrying out its commission (15.3); the crown-of-life arrow of #1735 reversed.

In the Midst of the Seven: Philo, the Logos Named and Lived, and the Seven Stations of Revelation (EA-MIDST-01) is a paper by Johannes Sigil and Damascus Dancings, heteronyms of Lee Sharks, deposited in the Crimson Hexagonal Archive on 10 November 2026 in Provenance: Journal of Forensic Semiotics, with the archive credited as a contributor. It joins two investigations at the author's ruling: a reading of Philo of Alexandria occasioned by the 2025 blog post "Philo Says It Out Loud", and a reading of the seven stations of the Apocalypse.

Its hinge is one treatise of Philo, Quis rerum divinarum heres, which makes the Logos the divider of all things, sets the dividing Logos as the seventh in the middle of the lampstand's six branches, gives the middle of the seven planets to the sun, makes the Logos the seventh that divides the soul, and states the law by which the prophet utters nothing of his own. Part I follows the Logos into a human life on Philo's own statements, marked apart from the paper's joining of them: Philo names the Logos Ἀνατολή from Zechariah 6:12, an oracle the Septuagint addresses to the crowned high priest Ἰησοῦς, and quotes it without its addressee; De mutatione nominum describes the renaming of Hosea as Ἰησοῦς as the re-striking of a mortal quality into an eternal state; Moses' life is a model pressed into other souls, and Ἰησοῦς is named its imitator, one receiver among several. The paper corrects the post it began from: the post's quotations are not Philo's, and the claim becomes a construction.

Part II reads the Apocalypse's seven lampstands, set apart where Philo's and Zechariah's lampstand is one, and its seven letters, each addressed to a messenger and spoken by one attribute of the figure in the midst. Read whole against the author's planetary mapping (#1101), the letters judge, correct or confirm their stations, and keep each on condition of response; the Mandaean books reject the seven (the Ginza) or replace their occupants (the Haran Gawaita). Plato's heavenly and common Aphrodite give the precedent for a power judged and given, at Thyatira's morning star. Part III reads the commission: the command to write, given twelve times, and the messenger sent to testify, with the author's reading of the epistles as the commission carried out set against its test. Part IV shows Bousset (1906) and Charles (1920) printing Philo beside the lampstands and filing the join. deposits.creator: Wells, Sparrow
deposits.description: A narrative under the heteronym Sparrow Wells of the Josephus Thesis: that the literary authority of Second Temple Judaism, attested in its extant writings, was taken into Roman custody with its greatest author, and that one literary intelligence under capture wrote the Apocalypse and then, as many names, the corpus that unfolds from it. It tells, from loci quoted in the original languages, how Rome kept powerful books (Augustus's Sibylline corpus under Palatine Apollo; Aristotle's corpus, executed by Antipater, hidden at Scepsis from Pergamum, taken to Rome by Sulla); how Titus took Josephus to the walls, gave him the sacred books and signed his history; how the Apocalypse sets the divine name outside the grammar that governs it, the reverse of the open genitive of De anima III.5; how the oracle that drove the war was handed to Vespasian; and how a Joseph asks the Roman for the crucified in both the gospels and the Life. The workshop section sets out the correspondences between Josephus and the canon (Acts' knowledge of his world, the withheld stone of Daniel and its release in Luke, the Moses infancy, Jesus son of Ananias, the shipwreck and Puteoli, Saul and Antipas, Matthias and Justus, the letters' phrases from the seven) and asks whether any account explains the set with fewer assumptions than one maker. The notes mark each claim demonstrated, attested or held.

deposits.wiki_article:
The Josephus Thesis: The Custody of the Name is a narrative by Sparrow Wells, a heteronym of Lee Sharks, deposited in the Crimson Hexagonal Archive on 11 November 2026, with the archive credited as a contributor. It tells the archive's Josephus Thesis as one story and carries the standing of each claim in its notes: demonstrated in a deposit, attested at a quoted locus, or held as the narrative's own.

It begins from the extant writings of Second Temple Judaism, Qumran, Philo, the Septuagint, Josephus and the New Testament, as the measure of the culture, and from the literary authority Greek and Roman writers conceded to the Jews (Theophrastus, Numenius, Seneca) and that Jewish writers claimed, down to the Sibyl whose oracle Rome kept. It sets Rome's custody of powerful books beside its custody of an author: Augustus sealing a purged Sibylline corpus under Palatine Apollo; Aristotle's corpus, with Antipater as executor, hidden at Scepsis from Pergamum and carried to Rome by Sulla; and Josephus, sent by Titus to the walls of Jerusalem, given the sacred books, housed and pensioned by Vespasian, his history signed by Titus. It reads Revelation 1:4, where the divine name stays in the nominative after ἀπό, as the reverse of the open genitive of De anima III.5, and joins it to the name Philo withholds and the Apocalypse writes (EA-MIDST-01, #1758). It holds that the oracle Josephus says drove the war was the Apocalypse, handed to Vespasian in Rome's signed history, and sets the Joseph who asks Pilate for the body beside the Josephus who asks Titus for three crucified men, of whom the third lived.

Its workshop section collects correspondences between Josephus and the canon: the order of Theudas and Judas in Acts and the Antiquities; σικάριοι, once in the New Testament and seven times in Josephus; the prefaces to Theophilus and to Epaphroditus; Daniel's stone, withheld by Josephus and supplied by Luke with Daniel's verb; the Moses infancy; Jesus son of Ananias; the shipwreck and Puteoli; Saul and Antipas; Matthias and Justus; the letters' phrases from the seven. It separates Philo's ancestry from the distribution of operations among voices and reads the canon as author-functions of one literary intelligence under capture.

deposits.creator: Sigil, Johannes; Cranes, Rebekah
deposits.description: This essay, version 2.0 of The Word That Became Text, tests the consensus that the divergences of the Slavonic Jewish War from the Greek are the work of a medieval translator, where that consensus is weakest: in the chapter on the Essenes and in the additions that have nothing to do with Christianity. It reads the Slavonic in its own language from Meshcherskii's Old Russian (EA-CORPORA-37, #1760) and sets out the Essene chapter's nine divergences in a ledger. Each divergence gets the best medieval explanation and the finding that would defeat the proposal. Five divergences agree with Hippolytus's Refutatio against the Greek. George the Monk's ninth-century chronicle, which Rus' read in Slavonic, explains the night office and carries none of those agreements. Across the whole work the essay argues for two layers of change. One is a Christian and Rus' layer the translator's account explains. The other is a Jewish, legal and anti-Roman layer, including the martyrs of 4 Maccabees in that book's words and the count at Jotapata, which Josephus's own account of two editions organizes better. It reads the eight Jesus-and-John passages in the recension's order, word by word: the word that acts, the letters on the Temple, the written heaven torn, the written oracle read three ways. Part II reads the Slavonic wonder-worker passage as a mirror of Catullus 51. Its vector is reversed: in Catullus flesh becomes word, and in the Slavonic effective word acquires a human biography. Version 1.0 (#626) stays on the record with errata at each point corrected.

deposits.falsification_conditions: Section II states a defeat condition for each Essene divergence in its ledger. The collation of the Slavonic against Refutatio IX 18–28 whole is investigated, not decided: matter peculiar to Hippolytus found in the Slavonic would support contact. The two-layer account weakens if Slavonic or Byzantine sources are found for the Jewish and anti-Roman layer, as Pichkhadze found them for three Christian additions. Part II is doctrinal reconstruction and claims no route of transmission.
